I found several open-source CLI tools that do this. The best fit depends on whether you need reversible tokens, a Rust or Python install, or a check-only mode.

- **leakguard** (Rust, zero dependencies) redacts secrets and PII from stdin or files and writes to stdout. It has a `--check` mode that exits non-zero when it finds anything, and it can limit detection to specific kinds such as email and IPv4. Fast, zero-dependency redaction of secrets and PII (emails, credit cards, IPs, JWTs, API keys, and more) from text and logs.
- **local-redact** (Python package and CLI) handles emails, IPs, API keys, and several regional IDs. Its stdin-to-stdout mode is cat app.log | local-redact redact > app.redacted.log. It also offers a `--check` flag and a JSON report, and its project description says it runs in your browser, so it may also have a no-install option.
- **hexredact** is aimed at logs and supports reversible redaction. It reads from stdin via `-`, and UI output goes to stderr, so stdout carries only the redacted text. It also gives the same value always the same token, so you can still follow one IP or user through the logs.
- **cleansh** (Rust) is built for terminal output and redacts sensitive information such as emails, IP addresses, various tokens (JWTs, AWS, GCP), SSH keys, hex secrets. Its docs show piping from docker logs my-sensitive-container | cleansh.
- **rog7/redact** (Python) is smaller in scope. It covers emails, API keys, and tokens, and the cleaned log is printed to stdout.

Detection coverage varies, so test any tool on a sample of your own logs before relying on it for secrets. Also note that sumankrsh/local-redact's README points out that Presidio, a well-known open-source option, covers many countries but lists no UAE or Saudi identifiers.

content.content:
## leakguard CLI Usage

**Overview:** `leakguard` is a command-line tool that redacts secrets and personal data (emails, credit cards, IPs, JWTs, API keys, and more) from text and logs.

**Basic usage:** `leakguard [OPTIONS] [FILES...]`

**stdin/stdout behavior:** With no file arguments, it reads stdin and writes redacted text to stdout. Line endings are preserved, and multiline PEM private keys are redacted as a single block. A `-` argument also reads stdin.

**Common examples from the page:**
- `tail -f app.log | leakguard`
- `leakguard access.log > clean.log`
- `leakguard --mask char --only email,ipv4 < input.txt`
- `leakguard --without phone app.log`
- `cat data.txt | leakguard --check --verbose`
- `tail -f app.log | leakguard --json`

**Masking options:**
- `--mask <MODE>`: `label` (default), `fixed`, `char`, `partial`, `hash`, or `template`
- `--template <STR>`: template for `--mask template` (default `<{LABEL}>`)
- `--fixed <STR>`: replacement for `--mask fixed` (default `[REDACTED]`)
- `--char <C>`: fill character for `char` and `partial` masks (default `*`)
- `--keep <N>`: characters to keep for `partial` (default 4, clamped to at most half the match)

**Detection options:**
- `--only <LIST>`: detect only the listed kinds
- `--without <LIST>`: skip listed kinds (`--exclude` is an alias)
- `--ignore <LIST>` and `--ignore-file <F>`: allowlist literal strings
- `--redact-word <W>`: redact a word or phrase as `[REDACTED:KEYWORD]`
- `--redact-literal <S>`: redact a literal, optionally with a kind (`WORD` or `WORD:KIND`)
- `--redact-words-file <F>`: read newline-separated words to redact

**Output options:**
- `--format <FMT>` or `--json`: NDJSON output with one object per input chunk. Matched values are omitted unless `--show-values` is set.
- `--stats`: print a redaction summary to stderr
- `--check`: print nothing; exit 1 if sensitive data is found
- `-v, --verbose`: with `--check`, print one line per finding to stderr (kind, offsets, line, and column, never values)

**Exit status:**
- `0`: no sensitive data found
- `1`: sensitive data found under `--check`
- `2`: usage error, unreadable file, or I/O error

**Detection kinds:**
- email
- credit_card
- ipv4
- ipv6
- jwt
- us_ssn
- mac
- aws_access_key
- url_credentials
- phone
- github_token
- slack_token
- stripe_key
- google_api_key
- openai_key
- private_key
- iban
- azure_connection_string
- telegram_token
- discord_token
- generic_secret (opt-in high-entropy scan)

Run `leakguard --list-kinds` to print these names.

**Replacement format:**
- Default `label` mask: the page does not spell out the exact default label output.
- `--mask fixed`: `[REDACTED]` by default.
- `--mask template`: `<{LABEL}>` by default.
- Keyword redactions from `--redact-word` and `--redact-literal` appear as `[REDACTED:KEYWORD]`, or `[REDACTED:KIND]` when a kind is given.

**License:** The page content does not state a license.

**Install command:** The page content does not include an install command.

content.content:
**hexredact** is an MIT-licensed Python tool that redacts PII, secrets, and infrastructure identifiers from log files.

**Install**
- `pipx install git+https://github.com/happygream/hexredact`
- Or run `pip install .` from a clone.
- Or run `python -m hexredact` from `src/` without installing.
- It needs Python 3.9+ and has no third-party dependencies. The README describes it as "Pure Python 3.9+ standard library."

**CLI usage**
- `hexredact` with no arguments opens an interactive wizard.
- `hexredact scan <path> --show 10` is a dry run that shows a before/after sample and writes nothing.
- `hexredact redact <path>` writes a redacted copy and keeps an untouched original.
- `hexredact lookup <map> '<token>'` reverses a token, and `hexredact restore <map> <dir>` restores a whole directory.
- `hexredact detectors` lists detectors. `--only`, `--disable`, `--mode mask`, `--terms`, `--allow`, and `--strict` adjust behavior.

**Stdin/stdout**
- Use `-` as the input to read from stdin, for example `journalctl -b | hexredact redact - --map boot.map.json`.
- UI output goes to stderr, so stdout carries only the redacted text and works in pipelines.

**What it detects**
- **Secrets:** JWTs, bearer tokens, and API keys for several services (AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe, OpenAI, Anthropic, and others), plus PEM keys and `password=`-style values.
- **People:** emails, phone numbers, payment cards, IBANs, national IDs (UK NI, US SSN), postcodes, and coordinates.
- **Network:** IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, MAC addresses, hostnames, and UNC paths.
- **Identity:** usernames in sshd/sudo/PAM contexts, Windows SIDs, and AWS account IDs.
- **IDs:** UUIDs, long hex strings, and long base64 blobs.

The README reports 31 detectors in total. It also offers reversible tokenization by default and a `mask` mode for irreversible redaction. Its own security notes say pattern-based redaction can miss things, so it recommends the residual scan and checking new log formats before sharing output.

**Maturity**
The repo is early-stage. It has 5 commits, 0 stars, 0 forks, and no releases listed. It does include a changelog, a test suite, CI workflows, and a security policy.

content.text:
I recommend **leakguard**. It's a free, open-source command-line filter that reads logs from stdin and writes a scrubbed copy to stdout, entirely on your machine. Detection patterns are built in, so you don't write any regexes.

I haven't installed or tested it. pickfit had nothing tested that fit this job, so this recommendation is based on the tool's published documentation.

## Main pick: leakguard (Rust, MIT/Apache-2.0)

- **License and release:** dual MIT/Apache-2.0. Version 1.0.0 came out on 2026-10-06. Source: https://github.com/ptukovar/leakguard
- **How it works:** with no file arguments, it reads stdin and writes redacted text to stdout. It keeps line endings and removes a multi-line PEM private key as a single block.
- **What it detects:** emails, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, JWTs, AWS access keys, GitHub, Slack, Stripe, Google, OpenAI, Telegram and Discord tokens, Azure connection strings, credentials inside URLs, private keys, credit cards, IBANs, phone numbers, US SSNs and MAC addresses.
- **One catch:** "generic_secret", a high-entropy scan for tokens it doesn't recognise by format, is **off by default**. If your logs contain your own app's tokens or session IDs, turn it on. Run `leakguard --help` to see exactly how.

### Install
I'm assuming you have the Rust toolchain (`cargo`). If you don't, install it from https://rustup.rs. Note that the standard rustup installer downloads a script and runs it in your shell, so read it first if you prefer.

```bash
cargo install leakguard        # puts the binary in ~/.cargo/bin/leakguard
leakguard --list-kinds         # confirm it works and see the detector names
```

### First run
```bash
# 1. Dry check: prints nothing, exits 1 if it finds anything sensitive.
#    -v lists each finding's type and position on stderr, never the value itself.
leakguard --check -v < server.log

# 2. Scrub and look at the result before pasting
leakguard server.log > server.clean.log
less server.clean.log

# 3. Common pipeline uses
journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago" | leakguard > for-ai.txt
leakguard --stats server.log > clean.log         # summary of what it removed goes to stderr
leakguard --ignore 127.0.0.1,example.com app.log # leave known-safe values alone
leakguard --redact-word acme-internal app.log    # also hide your company or host names
```
Other replacement styles are available with `--mask`: `fixed` gives `[REDACTED]`, and `partial` keeps the last few characters.

## Alternatives
- **hexredact** (Python 3.9+, MIT, uses only the standard library). It has 31 detectors, including hostnames, UUIDs, usernames in sshd/sudo logs, and API keys for services like Anthropic and OpenAI. By default it replaces each value with the same token every time, so you can still follow one IP or user through the log, and you can map the AI's answer back to the real values. It's very new: 5 commits, no releases.
  ```bash
  pipx install git+https://github.com/happygream/hexredact
  cat server.log | hexredact redact - --map server.map.json > clean.log
  # add --mode mask if you want removal that can't be reversed
  ```
- **cleansh** (Rust) and **local-redact** (Python) work as stdin-to-stdout filters in the same way. They're worth trying if leakguard misses something in your log format.
- **Gitleaks** is well known, but it only *reports* secrets. It doesn't output a scrubbed copy of your text, so it doesn't fit this job.

## A caveat for any of these
These tools match patterns. They will miss secrets in formats they don't know, such as your own tokens, internal hostnames or customer IDs. Before you rely on one:
1. Run it once on a real sample log and compare the input and output, for example with `diff server.log clean.log | less`.
2. Add `--redact-word` or `--ignore` rules for your own terms.
3. Still skim the output before each paste.

Sources:
- [leakguard on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest)
- [leakguard CLI source](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest/source/src/bin/leakguard.rs)
- [hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact)
- [cleansh](https://docs.rs/cleansh/0.1.7/i686-unknown-linux-gnu/cleansh/)
- [local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)
- [rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)

```bash
journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago" | leakguard > for-ai.txt
leakguard --stats server.log > clean.log         # summary of what it removed goes to stderr
leakguard --ignore 127.0.0.1,example.com app.log # leave known-safe values alone
leakguard --redact-word acme-internal app.log    # also hide your company or host names
```
Other replacement styles are available with `--mask`: `fixed` gives `[REDACTED]`, and `partial` keeps the last few characters.

## Alternatives
- **hexredact** (Python 3.9+, MIT, uses only the standard library). It has 31 detectors, including hostnames, UUIDs, usernames in sshd/sudo logs, and API keys for services like Anthropic and OpenAI. By default it replaces each value with the same token every time, so you can still follow one IP or user through the log, and you can map the AI's answer back to the real values. It's very new: 5 commits, no releases.
  ```bash
  pipx install git+https://github.com/happygream/hexredact
  cat server.log | hexredact redact - --map server.map.json > clean.log
  # add --mode mask if you want removal that can't be reversed
  ```
- **cleansh** (Rust) and **local-redact** (Python) work as stdin-to-stdout filters in the same way. They're worth trying if leakguard misses something in your log format.
- **Gitleaks** is well known, but it only *reports* secrets. It doesn't output a scrubbed copy of your text, so it doesn't fit this job.

## A caveat for any of these
These tools match patterns. They will miss secrets in formats they don't know, such as your own tokens, internal hostnames or customer IDs. Before you rely on one:
1. Run it once on a real sample log and compare the input and output, for example with `diff server.log clean.log | less`.
2. Add `--redact-word` or `--ignore` rules for your own terms.
3. Still skim the output before each paste.
